## Big Question {.role-slide}

How should a model represent responses that repeat participants, linguistic items, passages, or other sampled units?

## Data {.role-slide}

Sixty participants each judge several of forty sentence items. The table has 2,400 rows, but it does not contain 2,400 unrelated pieces of information.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Responses from one participant may share a scale-use tendency. Responses to one sentence may share an item difficulty.

## This Module {.role-slide .compact}

1. Identify repeated and sampled units.
2. Model group-specific baselines and contrasts.
3. Combine random effects with nonnormal responses.
4. Distinguish conditional from population variation.

## Repeated units in linguistic data {.section-slide}

The design comes before the formula

## Question {.role-slide}

Which rows share a participant, item, passage, speaker, language, or other sampled unit?

## Answer {.role-slide}

Participants and items are [**crossed**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) when each participant encounters several items and each item is encountered by several participants.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Hierarchical models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Name the response row, every repeated sampled unit, whether units are crossed or nested, and the populations across which the claim should generalize.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/structured-data.html)

## Population comparisons and sampled variation {.section-slide}

Fixed effects and random effects

## Goal {.role-slide}

Estimate a population condition comparison while representing persistent differences among sampled participants and linguistic items.

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Fixed effects**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) are population-level coefficients. [**Random effects**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) are group deviations modeled as draws from a population distribution.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Hierarchical models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A categorical predictor may be a fixed effect, while a participant identifier indexes random effects. Storage type does not determine the distinction.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/fixed-and-random-effects.html)

## Random effects and partial pooling {.section-slide}

Learning group deviations jointly

## Possibility {.role-slide}

Complete pooling ignores persistent speaker differences. No pooling estimates an unrelated baseline for every speaker.

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Partial pooling**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) estimates group deviations jointly with their population distribution. Sparsely observed groups move more toward the population center.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Hierarchical models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

This [**shrinkage**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) follows from the joint probability model. It is not a correction applied after estimating unrelated group means.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/random-effects.html)

## Random intercept models {.section-slide}

Group-specific baselines

## Method {.role-slide}

A [**random-intercept model**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) writes

$$
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0j}+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
b_{0j}\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_0^2).
$$

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Hierarchical models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

Two responses from group $j$ share $b_{0j}$. Crossed participant and item intercepts represent two distinct shared deviations.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A random intercept changes baselines across groups while retaining one common modeled predictor association.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/random-intercepts.html)

## Intraclass correlation {.section-slide}

Model-implied association within groups

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [**intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat502/Lesson06) for a linear random-intercept model is

$$
\operatorname{ICC}=\frac{\tau_0^2}{\tau_0^2+\sigma^2}.
$$

<div class="source">Penn State STAT 502</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat502/Lesson06
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

The numerator is shared group variance. The denominator is total variance for one response under the specified model.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The ICC describes the fitted model and grouping level. It is not a design-free property of the response variable.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/intraclass-correlation.html)

## Group-specific estimates {.section-slide}

Displaying partially pooled deviations

## Output {.role-slide}

Frequentist software often reports group deviations as [**conditional modes**](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/ranef.html). “Group-specific estimates” is the more general description.

<div class="source">lme4 reference</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/ranef.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

Display each deviation with its uncertainty and add the fixed intercept only when the scientific question concerns each group’s fitted baseline.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Do not turn a display of group estimates into many unadjusted tests or a certain ranking of weakly distinguished groups.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/random-effect-estimates.html)

## Random slope models {.section-slide}

Group-specific predictor associations

## Challenge {.role-slide}

A random-intercept model lets listeners differ in baseline responses but imposes one common condition contrast.

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**random-slope model**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) allows the association to vary by group.

$$
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+b_{0j}+(\beta_1+b_{1j})x_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}
$$

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Hierarchical models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

The predictor must vary within enough groups to inform slope variation. A predictor can vary in the complete table while remaining constant within each listener.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/random-slopes.html)

## Correlations among random effects {.section-slide}

Relating baseline and slope deviations

## Question {.role-slide}

Do groups with higher fitted baselines also tend to have larger or smaller fitted condition contrasts?

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**random-effects correlation**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) represents the population relation among random intercept and slope deviations.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Hierarchical models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The intercept definition determines the meaning of its correlation with the slope. Centering and contrast coding therefore affect interpretation.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/random-effect-correlations.html)

## Singular mixed model fits {.section-slide}

Lower-rank covariance estimates

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**singular fit**](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/isSingular.html) occurs when the estimated random-effects covariance matrix has lower rank than the specification permits.

<div class="source">lme4 reference</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/isSingular.html
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

Inspect within-group predictor variation, numbers of groups and observations, variance estimates, correlations, and estimated covariance dimensions.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Singularity is not the same as optimizer nonconvergence. Revise the population model deliberately and report the diagnosed dimension.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/singular-fits.html)

## Generalized linear mixed models {.section-slide}

Combining a GLM with random effects

## Method {.role-slide}

A [**generalized linear mixed model**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) places random effects inside the [generalized linear model](../../regression-models/generalized-linear-models.html) linear predictor.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Hierarchical models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

Recall the [logistic response model](../../regression-models/logistic-regression.html):

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0j}.
$$

The response remains Bernoulli. The participant baseline changes.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Predictions must state whether they condition on observed group estimates, set deviations to zero, or average over a group population.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/generalized-linear-mixed-models.html)

## Ordinal mixed models {.section-slide}

Ordered responses with crossed groups

## Method {.role-slide}

An [**ordinal mixed model**](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/articles/brms_families.html) places participant and discourse deviations inside the [cumulative-link](../../regression-models/ordinal-regression.html) location predictor.

<div class="source">brms family reference</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/articles/brms_families.html
:::

## Data {.role-slide}

Participants rate several discourses on *no*, *maybe*, and *yes*. Each discourse receives judgments from several participants.

<div class="source">de Marneffe, Simons, and Tonhauser 2019</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://ojs.ub.uni-konstanz.de/sub/index.php/sub/article/view/601
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Random intercepts represent baseline category use and discourse difficulty. They do not repair a failed proportional-odds assumption or missing slope variation.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.html)

## Bounded similarity judgments {.section-slide}

Aspectual similarity and sense similarity

## Data {.role-slide}

The teaching extract contains 4,405 ratings from 202 participants, 14 verbs, and 218 sentence pairs. Exact endpoints account for 20.8 percent of responses.

<div class="source">White, Grimm, and Glass 2026</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. ../../readings/white-grimm-glass-2026-aspectual-similarity.pdf
:::

## Result #1 {.role-slide}

Same-sense pairs average 55.9 in dissimilarity, compared with 76.4 for different-sense pairs. A linear mixed model estimates a 20.1-point decrease.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

The linear mixed model places 10.1 percent of fixed-effect predictive mass outside the 0 to 100 scale.

## Result #2 {.role-slide}

[Ordered-beta regression](../../regression-models/ordered-beta-regression.html) preserves the same direction and predicts endpoint mass near the observed 20.8 percent. Its latent coefficient is not measured in slider points.

<div class="source">Grove and White 2025; Kubinec 2023</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2022.20
2. ../../readings/white-grimm-glass-2026-aspectual-similarity.pdf
:::

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/aspectual-similarity-example.html)

## The Laplace approximation {.section-slide}

Integrating over random effects

## Challenge {.role-slide}

The marginal likelihood of a logistic or Poisson mixed model integrates over group deviations, and the integral usually has no simple formula.

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [**Laplace approximation**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-complexstan.html) replaces the log integrand near its mode with a quadratic function that can be integrated.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Complex Stan models</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-complexstan.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The approximation is a computational method, not a response model. Sparse groups and nonquadratic local shapes may make it inaccurate.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/laplace-approximation.html)

## Poisson mixed-effects models {.section-slide}

Counts, exposure, and repeated speakers

## Data {.role-slide}

A corpus counts filled pauses in interview segments. Segment duration varies, and each speaker contributes several segments.

## Method {.role-slide}

A [**Poisson mixed-effects model**](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/glmer.html) may use

$$
\log\lambda_{ij}=\log t_{ij}+\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0j}.
$$

<div class="source">lme4 reference</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/glmer.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The offset represents observation time. The fixed coefficient represents the population rate association. The random intercept represents persistent speaker rate differences.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/poisson-mixed-models.html)

## Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion {.section-slide}

Conditioning changes the variance statement

## Question {.role-slide}

How can counts be conditionally Poisson while their population variance exceeds their population mean?

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [law of total variance](../../random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.html) separates expected within-speaker variance from variance in expected counts across speakers.

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E_b[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid b)]+\operatorname{Var}_b[\mathbb E(Y\mid b)]
$$

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Random intercepts can produce marginal overdispersion and association among rows from one speaker. Overdispersion alone does not license a grouping term.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/overdispersion-and-random-effects.html)

## Conclusion {.section-slide}

Repeated participants and linguistic items

## Big Question {.role-slide}

How should a model represent responses that repeat participants, linguistic items, passages, or other sampled units?

## Answer {.role-slide .compact}

1. Identify repeated units before writing the model.
2. Separate population coefficients from group deviations.
3. Add slope variation only where the design contains the contrast.
4. State whether predictions condition on or average over group effects.
